description: Working on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator. Open to teammates, especially design or video.
summary: At the Moon's south pole, sunlight is a small target, and landers miss. A lander there lives on sunlight, but the Sun only skims the horizon, so lit ground lies right beside dark ground — and no lander comes down exactly where it aims (SLIM missed by 55 m, IM-2 by more than 400 m). TerminatorLine answers the question a mission planner actually has: for every possible landing date of 2027–28, on how many dates can a lander count on two weeks of sunlight anywhere in the circle it may come down in, not just at the point it aims at? We compute this across the whole pole on 20 m terrain for landing accuracies from 50 m to 1 km, and show each answer with what checks it: a year of LRO camera images, a finer 5 m map, real landers. The site is a 3D Moon, a pole map with a landing-accuracy slider, and a 3D view of the ground at each site with the light at any hour — a navigator for where, and on which date, to land.
details:
The question. Near the south pole the Sun only skims the horizon, so lit ground lies next to dark ground, and a lander lives on sunlight. Published landing sites are points; real landings are circles: SLIM came down 55 m from its target in 2024, IM-2 more than 400 m away in 2025. TerminatorLine asks, for each landing date, whether a lander gets its light anywhere it may actually come down.

What it computes. For every cell of a 20 m terrain model we compute where a solar panel 2 m above the ground sees the Sun, every six hours through 2027–28. A landing date works when the lander gets 14 days of sunlight with at most 48 hours of dark at a time. A site works on that date when nine landings in ten, scattered around the aim point with the chosen accuracy as 3σ, would get it. The result is the share of landing dates that work, per site and per cell, for accuracies from 50 m to 1 km. The whole pole south of 83.5° S was screened at 500 m, refined at 100 m on 43.8 % of it, and at 20 m on 3 780 km² around the candidate sites.

What it shows. Shackleton's rim works on 65 % of the dates if you hit the spot, 51 % within 100 m, 0 % within 250 m. Across the pole, if you can land within 100 m, 0.34 km² of ground works on at least half the dates; at 250 m no examined place does (the best reaches 47 %). 30 places work on half the dates, 323 more on a quarter. A ridge gives long light and forgives nothing; a plain forgives a miss and gives one lunar day.

What checks it. The model's lit/dark pattern is compared pixel by pixel with LRO's own camera record — the LROC WAC polar illumination maps, built from a year of images — and with LOLA's long-term visibility maps; the 20 m result is re-computed on NASA's 5 m maps where they exist; and real landers' misses are drawn on the map. Where the camera disagrees or no camera map exists, the site says so.

The site. A 3D Moon with the true directions of Sun and Earth, a pole map with the landing-accuracy slider, and a 3D view of the ground at each site with the light at any hour. Everything is computed ahead of time and served as static files; the method, sources and limits are on the Data and method page.

Tools. Computation in Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio/GDAL, Skyfield with NAIF SPICE kernels); website in TypeScript with React, three.js, zustand and Vite; tests with Vitest and Playwright.

Use of AI. AI coding assistants (Claude, through Claude Code) wrote most of the code and drafted the site's text under our direction; the question, the method, the design decisions, the checks against LRO imagery and every judgement call are ours. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used: every picture on the site is rendered from the data. AI-written code is declared in the repository README.
